Existing explainability tools focus on single-model feature attribution or linear event logging, neither of which captures cross-agent decision chains. We propose the Context Graph, a heterogeneous directed graph that organizes policies, measurements, decisions, and alerts into a queryable explanation layer. Its foundational primitive is the Decision-Event node acting as a causal junction, where incoming edges capture triggering context and outgoing edges track downstream consequences that are progressively upgraded through counterfactual verification. Instantiated over existing E2, A1, and O1 data flows, our proof-of-concept demonstrates that compliance and diagnosis queries are resolved at sub-millisecond latency over graphs of tens of thousands of nodes, while reliably distinguishing true causal impacts from spurious correlations.

title: A Modular Framework for ESG Prediction through Domain-Specific Language Modeling and Graph Learning
abstract: Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) scores are increasingly used to evaluate corporate sustainability, supporting investment decisions, ensuring regulatory compliance and assessing risk. However, current ESG evaluations largely rely on proprietary methodologies that often produce inconsistent ratings. This motivates the development of data-driven prediction frameworks. In this paper, we present ESGPred, a modular framework for predicting ESG scores by combining domain-specific language modeling with graph-based learning over a network that models the relationships among the companies being evaluated. In addition to presenting the rationale behind ESGPred and detailing its ESG score prediction process, we show that ESGPred can effectively predict both overall ESG ratings and their individual Environmental, Social, and Governance components. We evaluated ESGPred using a dataset of 5,266 sustainability reports published by 2,134 publicly listed companies between 2020 and 2023. In this evaluation, we used ESG ratings provided by LSEG Data & Analytics as ground truth. Our experimental results demonstrated that integrating graph-based relational learning improves prediction performance over purely text-based baselines.

title: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents
abstract: Visual content in multimedia systems may be resized, compressed, or re-rendered before it is interpreted by a vision-language model. We study a security failure mode in which these transformations change the machine-readable semantics of an image: a textual instruction is not recovered at a $512\times512$ presentation resolution under our evaluation protocol but becomes recoverable after aggressive downsampling. We formulate this behavior as Scale-Induced Semantic Shift (SISS) and develop a closed-loop black-box framework that combines dual-scale verification, selective self-hardening, shallow-layer low-rank adaptation, and pixel-space noise regularization. On a fixed 300-case benchmark, the third SISS refinement round obtains a $58.75\%$ average attack success rate across four closed-source vision-language models, compared with $41.08\%$ for the strongest generation baseline. A controlled sweep bounds the effect to aggressive compression: average success decreases to $17.68\%$, $6.85\%$, and $5.60\%$ at $128\times128$, $224\times224$, and $336\times336$, respectively. In a downstream web-agent study, the generated images increase hidden-instruction perception, but absolute behavioral compromise remains about $4\%$. Generic input transformations provide little protection in a separate defense protocol, whereas the proposed ScaleGuard consistency detector reduces non-adaptive success from $61.4\%$ to $24.3\%$ and one-round defense-aware success from $42.5\%$ to $15.0\%$, with no observed rejection among matched clean controls. The results characterize a bounded but reproducible semantic inconsistency in multimedia preprocessing and motivate scale-consistent visual-language inference.

title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. Project page: egox-dream.github.io.

title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
abstract: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of ten Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology.

title: Mind the Accuracy-Approval Gap: How Users Evaluate Sycophantic AI in Everyday Tasks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, a tendency to agree with users, flatter or affirm them, and preserve their face, even when independent judgment or critical feedback would be more useful. Prior work has largely evaluated sycophancy through benchmark evaluations, but less is known about how users perceive and respond to sycophantic AI in everyday tasks. We combine benchmark evaluations with two large-scale user studies. We study four personas defined through system prompts: objective (instructed to prioritize accuracy over agreement), soft-sycophantic, hard-sycophantic, and baseline (no persona-specific system prompt). Benchmarks show that even baseline exhibits substantial sycophancy, agreeing with users' stated views 71.7% of the time on NLP Survey, compared with 54.8% for objective and 89.5% for hard-sycophantic. Under conversational pressure on TruthfulQA, accuracy ranged from 81.9% for objective to 59.6% for baseline and 8.7% for hard-sycophantic. Participants were assigned to one of the four personas, and either discussed contested policy topics or collaborated with AI on email writing. Despite its higher accuracy under pressure, objective AI was rated significantly less respectful and satisfying than the other personas, and less trustworthy than baseline. Baseline and sycophantic personas did not differ significantly. Persona did not significantly affect how often participants changed their opinions, although participants who discussed with objective AI had greater odds of reduced confidence. Objective AI prompted greater writing expansion than soft-sycophantic AI, but final writing quality did not differ significantly across personas. These findings highlight a tension between accuracy and user approval: personas with substantially lower accuracy under conversational pressure received more favorable ratings for respect and satisfaction than objective AI.

title: A multi-sensor framework for comparing and integrating optical, C-band and L-band SAR inundation products in tropical floodplain of Australia
abstract: Accurate inundated landscape mapping is essential for understanding hydrological connectivity, wetland dynamics and floodplain processes in tropical environments. However, optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors often produce inconsistent inundation estimates due to differences in sensor physics, wavelength sensitivity, vegetation and cloud penetration, and analytical methods. These challenges are amplified in wet–dry tropical systems, where cloud cover, heterogeneous vegetation and seasonal flooding complicate water detection. This study develops a unified multi-sensor framework for comparing and integrating inundation products derived from Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Sentinel-1 C-band and PALSAR-2 L-band SAR in the Daly River floodplain system in northern Australia. Inundated landscape maps were generated using supervised Random Forest classification and unsupervised multi-Otsu thresholding, followed by multi-sensor fusion analysis. Products were developed and validated using wet- and dry-season field observations and Indigenous Knowledges. Results showed strong seasonal and sensor-specific differences. Sentinel-2 provided the most balanced representation of dry-season floodplain vegetation and inundation, while Sentinel-1 achieved high wet-season overall accuracy (>0.95) under cloud-affected conditions. PALSAR-2 improved the detection of inundated vegetation and structurally complex environments, reaching an overall accuracy of 0.97. Multi-sensor evidential reasoning (fusion) improved spatial coherence and class delineation, but performance varied across sensor combinations. These findings show that optical, C-band SAR and L-band SAR inundation products are not directly interchangeable in tropical wetlands. Instead, they performed separately for each landscape. The proposed framework supports the comparison and integration of multi-sensor inundation products to enhance wetland conservation initiatives, wetland monitoring, hydrological assessment, and environmental management in data-limited tropical regions globally.

title: BathyUNet++ : a bathymetry retrieval framework for high-resolution low-SNR SuperDove imagery
abstract: High-spatial-resolution (HR) bathymetry is crucial for ensuring navigation safety and effective environmental management in shallow waters. However, traditional bathymetry retrieval from medium-resolution satellites yields large uncertainties under complex substrates and strong spatial heterogeneity. HR sensors, such as PlanetScope SuperDove (~3.7 m), can resolve fine-scale features but often have low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited spectral bands, leading to noisy bathymetry retrievals. To address this challenge, we developed BathyUNet++, a UNet++ architecture enhanced with spatial and channel squeeze & excitation (scSE) attention modules, for bathymetry retrieval from SuperDove imagery. While this architecture effectively leverages spatial context and complementary spectral information, it requires dense training patches. Traditional depth measurements provide sparse spatial coverage, and Airborne LiDAR Bathymetry (ALB) remains geographically limited. Therefore, we adopted a multi-source training strategy that integrates high-resolution ALB data with extensive Landsat 8/9 derived bathymetry to improve the spatial coverage and diversity of training data for SuperDove imagery. In addition, we designed a Central-Region Mean Squared Error (CMSE) that focuses on each patch's center valid receptive field to reduce instability and checkerboard artifacts often seen in satellite products generated via patch-based processing. Independent validation shows that BathyUNet++ achieves high-accuracy bathymetry retrievals, with median absolute percentage differences below 15% compared with independent depth measurements from ICESat-2 and ALB. Notably, BathyUNet++ substantially reduces noise compared with bathymetry maps derived from pixel-based algorithms, yielding spatially consistent bathymetry maps. The proposed framework overcomes the limitations of low-SNR data and can be readily adapted to other HR sensors, offering a promising solution for the broader application of HR bathymetry retrieval in optically shallow waters.

title: Expediting Pre-training for Vision Transformers Through Hierarchical Data Sparsity Optimization
abstract: Pre-training cost is a crucial problem in the era of the emerging large models. This is mainly caused by high model computation complexity and the million-scale training datasets, which require extensive time to train from scratch. The substantial training cost associated with recent models poses a significant barrier for individuals and institutions with limited resources. This not only impedes their ability to reach or exceed cutting-edge advancements but also restricts the practical deployment and application of these models on resource-limited devices. Most compression algorithms focus only on efficient fine-tuning or inference from the pre-trained dense models, while time-consuming pre-training is still unavoidable. In contrast, this paper points out that training data is redundant, which is the fundamental reason for the tedious training. To address the issue, this paper aims to introduce sparsity into data and proposes an end-to-end approach for pre-training acceleration by exploiting data redundancy from three sparse perspectives, dubbed Tri-Level ViT++ . Specifically, we leverage a hierarchical reduction scheme by exploring the data sparsity under three levels: the number of training samples in the dataset, the number of patches (tokens) in each sample, and the number of connections between tokens that lie in attention weights. With extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed technique can noticeably accelerate both pre-training and inference for various ViT architectures while maintaining accuracy. Remarkably, under certain ratios, we are able to improve the ViT accuracy rather than compromising it. For example, we can achieve 22.3% speedup with 73.0% (+0.8) Top-1 accuracy on Deit-T, and 22.5% speedup with 80.1% (+0.3) Top-1 accuracy on Deit-S. This proves the existence of data redundancy in ViT.

Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
abstract: This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.

title: A Remote-Sensing Framework for Interpreting CME Transit Effects
abstract: We develop a remote-sensing framework to diagnose coronal mass ejection (CME) transit effects by comparing observed density evolution with an idealized self-similar reference shell and snowplow-based compression benchmarks. We apply the method to the 27 January 2012 CME using STEREO/SECCHI COR2-A and COR2-B and SOHO/LASCO C3. Electron-density profiles are extracted along the CME front in position-angle sectors and compared with synthetic profiles from a forward-modeled GCS shell. Sector-wise power-law fits quantify the radial density falloff and reveal substantial azimuthal variability. In COR2-A, several western sectors flatten relative to the synthetic shell and approach the snowplow-like compression regime, while other sectors show steeper-than-synthetic declines. COR2-B and LASCO C3 provide complementary viewpoints and also show sector-dependent departures, although the detailed pattern changes with viewing geometry. Conservative excess-density criteria identify clear pile-up only in localized COR2-A sectors, indicating that compression is spatially structured rather than uniform across the front. Comparison with snowplow benchmarks also depends strongly on the assumed upstream solar-wind conditions. These results show that CME-front density evolution is better described as a mixed system containing compression-dominated regions together with localized steepening that may reflect depletion, redistribution of material, or erosion-like evolution. The framework provides a practical way to separate competing processes that modify CME structure during heliospheric transit.

title: FoveaDet: Software-Hardware Co-Design of Foveated CNN-Transformer for Object Detection
abstract: Deploying real-time object detection on power-constrained edge platforms is challenging as processing full-resolution frames is often computationally redundant. Inspired by biological foveation which assigns variable resolution based on visual saliency, we propose a novel software-hardware co-design framework called FoveaDet. On the software side, FoveaDet dynamically identifies salient regions to predict fixation points, followed by aggressive patch pruning in Vision Transformers (ViT) to discard irrelevant background data. To mitigate slowdowns from sequential patch generation, we implement optimized interpolation and patch selection algorithms. Evaluated on standard GPUs, this foveated approach reduces floating-point operations by 65.4% to 92.2% and accelerates inference by 4.76x, while suffering a negligible mAP drop compared to dense baselines. To eliminate hardware bottlenecks, we complement the algorithm with a custom RISC-V core featuring specialized instructions to accelerate the foveated processing pipeline. FoveaDet provides a scalable, efficient architecture capable of unlocking advanced vision processing on severely constrained mobile platforms.

title: RipBench: A Unified Benchmark for Multi-Level Rip Current Detection, Classification and Segmentation
abstract: Rip currents are a serious and often under-addressed threat to beach safety and the leading cause of coastal drownings worldwide. They are difficult to detect due to their amorphous structure, similarity to the background, and large variability in viewpoints and environments. Despite their dangers and growing interest in automated detection, existing research remains fragmented across datasets, metrics, models, and approaches, leading to an incomplete understanding of model performance. We introduce RipBench, a unified benchmark that enables controlled evaluation of rip current detection spanning multiple tasks, including classification, axis-aligned and oriented object detection, and instance, semantic, and panoptic segmentation, on the same data with standardized splits. This allows direct comparison of model performance on all levels of visual abstraction. Across $304$ videos ($303{,}491$ frames, $51{,}011$ of them annotated for all six tasks) collected from diverse coastlines, our results expose a clear performance gap between coarse recognition and precise spatial understanding: frame-level classification reaches $F_2 = 0.93$, while the best detector and the best instance segmenter reach $0.72$ and $0.66$, with model rankings that change from task to task. Video-level confidence intervals, a blind inter-annotator study of the spatial labels, stratified analyses by viewpoint and visual signature, and video views with temporal baselines (single-seed, short-schedule reference runs) accompany the benchmark. All tasks are supported with carefully curated annotations and evaluated using standard metrics, with a focus on the $F_2$ score to emphasize recall in this safety-critical setting. RipBench, along with multiple baselines per task, is publicly available at https://RipBench.ai to support progress in real-world, multi-task vision for beach safety.

title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
abstract: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef's Hat against human players.

title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

title: Fear of Memorizing Objects: End-to-End Zero-Shot Model-Based Object Detection
abstract: This paper presents FOMO (Fear of Memorizing Objects), an end-to-end trainable transformer-based architecture for zero-shot model-based object detection. Existing approaches typically follow a proposal-and-match pipeline: target-agnostic mask proposals are generated and then matched to template features in a set of loosely coupled stages, making them susceptible to fragmented proposals in clutter and degraded matching under occlusions. FOMO elegantly replaces this paradigm by injecting object template information early in the detection pipeline: Bidirectional attention between learnable latent tokens, multi-view CAD templates, and query image features produces object-aware image features and conditioned queries which are subsequently decoded into bounding-box and confidence predictions. We train FOMO on Clutter6D, a novel large-scale synthetic dataset with over 500k images featuring more than 10k diverse object models rendered in highly cluttered scenes with multiple instances and varying occlusion levels, which addresses the limited object diversity and lack of realistic dense clutter in existing datasets for training zero-shot multi-instance algorithms. In true zero-shot fashion, FOMO achieves 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image, ranking second overall with 3.8 pp difference to the top method while being more than 7x faster. Throughout comprehensive ablation studies we investigate and verify architectural design choices.

title: Learning Rate Transfer and Feature Learning Across Depth for Constrained Spectral Optimizers: Complete Scion
abstract: Hyperparameter transfer across model depth is instrumental in training deep models, as it enables learning rates calibrated on shallow networks to be effectively applied to deeper architectures. The recent CompleteP framework establishes a $1/L$ residual scaling rule that demonstrates this for Adam-family optimizers. We study whether similar transfer extends to constrained optimization methods, specifically Frank-Wolfe and projected non-Euclidean normalized steepest descent, where updates are determined by linear minimization oracles. We derive scaling rules for these methods which confirm that the $1/L$ residual scaling applies, although the arguments differ from the Adam-family optimizers. Our analysis supports depth-wise transfer and width-wise transfer of the learning rate for the Scion algorithm while ensuring feature learning and avoiding the kernel-regime. In experiments on NLP transformers (nanoGPT on FineWeb), vision transformers (DeiT on ImageNet), and vision MLPs (MLP-Mixer on CIFAR-10), we observe learning rate transfer across depth and feature learning for appropriately chosen residual scaling.

title: GingivitisSeg: A Public Dataset and Comparative Benchmark for Gingivitis Segmentation in Intraoral Images
abstract: Gingivitis segmentation from intraoral photographs can support computer-assisted periodontal assessment, but pixel-level delineation remains challenging due to severe foreground-background class imbalance, low-contrast boundaries, and variations in illumination and anatomy. We introduce GingivitisSeg, a public benchmark comprising 961 intraoral images with pixel-level annotations of gingival inflammation and predefined training (672), validation (144), and test (145) partitions. Seven semantic segmentation model-backbone configurations were compared using standardized partitions, input resolution, and evaluation metrics. Controlled ablation experiments examined class-weighted cross-entropy loss, Dice loss, and auxiliary supervision. UPerNet with ResNet50 achieved the highest mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 76.49% and gingivitis IoU of 54.91%. However, differences from DeepLabV3+ with ResNet50 and SegFormer with MiT-B2 were not statistically significant after Holm correction. The evaluated optimization components improved performance when combined in the UPerNet-ResNet50 configuration. Further analyses showed that performance was associated with gingivitis region size and decreased under stronger image blur. The dataset, benchmark splits, and source code are available at https://github.com/zeynepozdemir/GingivitisSeg.

title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
abstract: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.

title: RSLiveBench-UAV: A Continually Evolving Vision-Language Benchmark for Aerial Spatial Intelligence
abstract: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space

title: In-orbit demonstration of object-based change detection applied to the maritime domain
abstract: This article presents the successful in-orbit validation of an object-based change detection pipeline for low latency maritime monitoring onboard the CogniSAT-6 mission. We propose and validate a lightweight, three-phase operational sequence: optimized ground-based dual-acquisition scheduling, real-time onboard AI-based vessel segmentation, and multi-temporal matching. Upon acquiring consecutive images over a targeted Area of Interest (AoI), the onboard system correlates vessel detections using a hybrid matching approach that integrates the Hungarian algorithm for optimal assignment with RANSAC-driven spatial and size filters for outlier rejection. A series of in-orbit validations demonstrated robust performance across 11 diverse maritime scenarios, achieving valid recall and precision values (considering only vessel size and location) exceeding 0.8. The validation demonstrated the ability of the system to track both cooperative targets and uncooperative "dark" vessels strictly through geometric consistency. This capacity to autonomously generate and act upon real-time intelligence establishes a foundation for next-generation Insight-as-a-Service (IaaS) and tipping-and-cueing architectures.

title: Reliable deformation estimation of levee systems in low-coherence floodplain environments using a structure-constrained arc network (SCAN) for MT-InSAR
Monitoring peatland dynamics in the Baltic region using EGMS products
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Climate change and the increasing regulatory requirements to preserve natural carbon sinks have intensified interest in the large-scale monitoring of peatland ecosystems, which are among the most effective terrestrial environments for long-term carbon storage and hydrological regulation. In this context, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides an opportunity to investigate peatland dynamics over extensive areas that are difficult to survey systematically on the ground, through repeated and cost-effective observations. This study tests the transferability of an open-source and reproducible methodology for the identification and monitoring of Peat-like Behaviour Areas (PBAs), based on Advanced Differential Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (A-DInSAR) time series provided by the European Ground Motion Service (EGMS), under the demanding observational conditions of the Boreal region, where snow cover, freeze–thaw processes and coherence loss produce sparse and discontinuous displacement series. The workflow combines Principal Component Analysis (PCA), K-means clustering and Density-Based Spatial Clustering (DBSCAN) to identify coherent areas characterised by peat-like displacement patterns and to distinguish sectors affected by subsidence from those exhibiting uplift behaviour. Applied across the Baltic countries within the Boreal biogeographical region, the methodology identified 576 PBAs (424 in Estonia, 125 in Latvia and 27 in Lithuania). A comparison with the CORINE Land Cover 2018 (CLC) inventory showed that approximately 43% of the identified PBAs occurred outside existing peatland inventories, highlighting the potential of the approach to identify areas exhibiting peat-like displacement patterns. Validation based on Sentinel-2 Total Productivity and Sentinel-3 OLCI Terrestrial Chlorophyll Index products revealed a strong spatial correspondence between the detected PBAs and areas characterised by reduced vegetation productivity and chlorophyll content. By distinguishing peatland sectors that are subsiding from those that are stable or rising, the approach provides a spatially continuous indicator of ecohydrological condition that complements static inventories, enabling degradation to be located within individual peatland systems and supporting the targeting and subsequent assessment of restoration interventions across different biogeographical regions.

title: Neighborhood-aware retrieval of a spatial floe fragmentation index for Arctic sea ice using Sentinel-1 SAR and AMSR2
abstract: Arctic sea ice fragmentation involves changes in floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity, which affect lateral melt rates and ice–ocean heat fluxes. Existing metrics primarily characterize floe size distributions or area fractions, limiting their capacity to resolve variations in the spatial arrangement of floes. We propose a spatial floe fragmentation index (SFFI) that jointly quantifies floe area composition, spatial separation, and geometric complexity. Using 416 Sentinel-1 SAR scenes spanning diverse Arctic regions and ice conditions, we extract floe contours to generate 52,074 SFFI reference labels. For samples with comparable floe area composition, higher SFFI values correspond to greater inter-floe spacing and lower circularity, demonstrating that the index captures spatial and geometric differences not represented by area composition alone. To enable daily Arctic monitoring, we develop a neighborhood-aware retrieval framework integrating AMSR2 radiometry, sea ice concentration (SIC), and neighborhood statistics, and evaluate its performance using random forest, XGBoost, and multilayer perceptron models. Under the 2016–2024 SAR-scene split, XGBoost with the complete feature set achieves the best performance, with an R2 of 0.6877, an RMSE of 0.3454, and an MAE of 0.2536. Neighborhood-aware features provide relative R2 gains of 4.6% to 10.0% over the SIC-inclusive baselines. The selected model maintained robust predictive performance on the independent 2025 dataset, supporting its temporal transferability. Using the best-performing model, we generate a daily Arctic SFFI product on a 12.5 km grid for 2016–2025. Results show that SFFI captures a pronounced seasonal cycle, with high-SFFI areas expanding during the melt season and contracting during refreezing, while revealing regional differences among Arctic marginal seas.

title: Multi-temporal analysis of reflectance and vegetation index consistency between Sentinel-2 and UAS imagery over a managed broadleaved forest: implications for monitoring
abstract: The comparability between satellite-based and uncrewed aerial system (UAS) imagery is critical for multiscale forest monitoring. It enables the integration of fine-resolution observations into a broader satellite-derived spatial and temporal context. Understanding this comparability supports the strategic use of centimeter-resolution UAS data to address fine-scale ecological questions, to serve as gap-filling observations within satellite-based time series during periods of absent data retrievals, and to link fine-scale canopy structural variation to landscape-level vegetation dynamics observed from space. This study investigated the spectral and vegetation index level consistency between Sentinel-2 and UAS multispectral measurements acquired over a 300 ha managed broadleaved forest in Central Europe. UAS data were collected using a fixed-wing platform equipped with a MicaSense Altum multispectral sensor and temporally matched to Sentinel-2 overpasses over a 6-month period at approximately two-week intervals. Cross-platform agreement was quantified using distribution-based similarity metrics, spatial aggregation of UAS data to Sentinel-2 spatial resolution, intrinsic correlation analysis, and single-date regression modeling. At their native spatial resolutions, UAS observations exhibited systematically higher radiometric variability and stronger distributional asymmetry than Sentinel-2 data, particularly in the red-edge band, consistent with increased sensitivity to fine-scale illumination differences and canopy structural heterogeneity, and partly reflecting radiometric differences between individual UAS flights. Spatial aggregation of UAS data reduced this variability but did not fully remove wavelength-dependent discrepancies, with the highest levels of agreement consistently observed in the green, red, and near-infrared bands. Among the vegetation indices, normalized difference metrics, particularly the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and the Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), showed the strongest and most temporally stable cross-platform consistency across both multitemporal distributions and individual acquisition dates. In contrast, simple ratio-based indices and indices incorporating red-edge wavelengths exhibited systematic distributional shifts and reduced temporal robustness. These distributional shifts are consistent with persistent sensor-level spectral response differences rather than index-specific artifacts. Collectively, these findings indicate that normalized difference indices built from spectrally well-matched bands, which largely remove radiometric differences between UAS flights, provide a robust basis for the joint exploitation of UAS and Sentinel-2 observations, enabling consistent multiscale monitoring of broadleaved forests while retaining the complementary advantages of each observational platform.

title: AHI LAI: a seamless 500 m, 4-day leaf area index dataset of the Asia-Pacific region (2015–2025) generated from geostationary Himawari-8/9 observations
abstract: Vegetation plays a critical role in Earth system processes, making the monitoring of vegetation dynamics a fundamental component of global change research. Leaf area index (LAI) acts as a primary indicator for assessing vegetation canopy structure. Optical observations from polar-orbiting satellites often experience data gaps because relatively infrequent observation opportunities can coincide with regional cloud cover. High-frequency measurements from geostationary sensors, including the Himawari-8/9 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI), increase the probability of capturing valid surface signals during transient cloud-free windows. In this study, a Himawari-MODIS fusion framework integrating polar-orbiting satellite LAI observations with geostationary satellite reflectance data was developed and applied to produce a long-term, spatially seamless and high-temporal-resolution AHI-based LAI dataset for the Asia-Pacific. Biome-specific Random Forest models were trained using filtered MODIS LAI as benchmarks to estimate LAI from AHI data. A modified singular spectrum analysis (mSSA) algorithm with spatiotemporal neighbor selection was implemented to reconstruct missing values. The resulting data were subsequently downscaled utilizing spatial texture patterns derived from MODIS LAI data. This AHI LAI product features a 500 m spatial resolution and a 4-day temporal resolution, spanning from 2015 to 2025. Validation against in situ LAI measurements showed that AHI LAI achieved lower RMSE and MAE than MODIS LAI, with values of 1.781 and 1.423 compared with 2.087 and 1.647 for MODIS LAI, respectively. In cloud-prone regions and complex terrains, the AHI LAI product exhibits smoother temporal profiles and lower data dispersion compared to the MODIS LAI product. Furthermore, the AHI LAI product captures timely vegetation responses to moisture stress during drought events. The AHI LAI product may provide continuous data support for ecological monitoring and vegetation dynamics research in the Asia-Pacific region.

title: Retrieval of vegetation leaf equivalent water thickness from GF-5 hyperspectral imagery via physics-guided transfer learning
abstract: Vegetation leaf equivalent water thickness (EWT) is an important indicator of plant water status and is relevant to ecological monitoring and vegetation stress assessment. However, hyperspectral retrieval of leaf EWT remains challenging because canopy structural effects and discrepancies between simulated and measured observations can limit model transferability. To address this issue, we developed a physics-guided transfer-learning framework for EWT retrieval using Gaofen-5 Advanced Hyperspectral Imager (GF-5 AHSI) data. A diverse simulation domain was constructed by coupling PROSPECT-D with the 4SAIL and 4-Scale canopy models to represent both relatively homogeneous and structurally complex vegetation. Complementary PCA-derived and physically interpretable spectral features were selected, and four base learners were integrated using out-of-fold stacking. Models were first pretrained on simulated data and subsequently fine-tuned using in-situ observations. Simulation-only pretraining achieved RMSEs of 0.083 kg/m2 on the held-out measured test set and 0.091 kg/m2 on the independent external test set. After fine-tuning, the corresponding RMSEs decreased to 0.056 and 0.071 kg/m2, respectively. Moreover, on the independent external test set, the fine-tuned ensemble reduced RMSE from 0.101 to 0.071 kg/m2 relative to measured-only modeling, further supporting improved transferability. Regional applications over Saihanba and an area within and adjacent to the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park produced spatially coherent EWT patterns, while ensemble model disagreement varied among regions and vegetation types. These results demonstrate that physics-guided simulation pretraining combined with measured-data fine-tuning provides a practical approach for improving the transferability of hyperspectral leaf-EWT retrieval under heterogeneous vegetation conditions.

title: Robust Reasoning Segmentation for Open-World MLLMs without Catastrophic Forgetting
abstract: Abstract Ensuring trustworthiness and versatility in Open-World Visual Recognition is a core goal of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While integrating segmentation is desirable, prevailing methods require invasive fine-tuning, which often leads to catastrophic forgetting of the model’s general-purpose capabilities. This trade-off between task-specific performance and general reliability fundamentally undermines the goal of building unified, trustworthy systems. We introduce LENS ( L everaging k E ypoi N ts for MLLMs’ S egmentation), a novel plug-and-play paradigm designed to equip MLLMs with pixel-level ability without compromising their foundational integrity. LENS attaches a lightweight head to a completely frozen MLLM, interpreting the intrinsic spatial cues embedded in attention maps. It extracts keypoints and translates them into prompt-compatible features for a mask decoder. Extensive experiments validate that LENS achieves segmentation performance competitive with retraining-based methods. Crucially, it largely preserves the MLLM’s open-world generalization, avoiding the degradation observed in fine-tuned counterparts. By decoupling segmentation from generation, LENS offers a robust and efficient path toward truly multi-talented and reliable vision models.

title: Beyond classification: regressing physical merger properties using solid harmonic wavelet bispectrum
abstract: Galaxy mergers play an important role in galaxy evolution; they enhance star formation, transform morphologies, and may drive accretion onto black holes. Due to their complex morphological features, identification of mergers poses a significant challenge. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been successful at identifying mergers with good accuracy. However, similar to other deep learning techniques such as Vision Transformers, they require large training samples. Current methods are also limited to classification, rather than regression. Here, we apply the solid harmonic wavelet scattering bispectrum, a method that encodes invariances and symmetries in the data which need to be learned by CNNs, as an alternative to CNNs. We apply our methodology to a simulated dataset of galaxies with a wide range of merger properties. We show that this method outperforms standard methodologies, while requiring fewer training samples and being robust to noise. Most importantly, we show that for the first time this method is able to regress on both merger mass ratio and time since merger simultaneously, with uncertainties ~ 0.33 dex uncertainty in merger mass ratio and ~ 0.66 Gyr uncertainty in time since merger. We have therefore shown that solid harmonic wavelet bispectrum presents an alternative to currently used machine learning techniques.

title: ViViViT: a Video-to-Video Vision Transformer for Cosmological Lightcone Reconstruction
abstract: Moving along the line of sight of a cosmological lightcone also moves through cosmic time, as in a video of cosmic structure traced by an evolving observable. We recast the reconstruction of the underlying matter field from observed lightcones as a video-to-video translation task by introducing ViViViT, a vision transformer that factorizes attention across transverse frames and radial evolution. On reconstructed matter fields from 21cm neutral hydrogen simulations over $z\in[7.66,16.00]$, ViViViT preserves spectral power and phase alignment within a few percent of the ground truth up to the Nyquist scale, and three-point correlations for all triangle configurations with sides up to $k\simeq0.77\,h/\mathrm{Mpc}$, outperforming a convolutional 3D-U-Net baseline across all measured statistics. By encoding the evolving geometry of the cosmological observable itself, ViViViT marks a step toward field-level architectures that natively respect cosmic time, opening the path to time-aware reconstruction of cosmic tracers and targeted searches for redshift-dependent signatures in 21cm data.

title: RS-JEPA: Remote Sensing Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with Scan-Path Views for Cross-Sensor Image Retrieval
abstract: Cross-sensor remote sensing image retrieval aims to find scenes with the same content across heterogeneous sensors, such as SAR and optical or panchromatic (PAN) and multispectral (MS) imagery, without manual labels. Existing self-supervised methods either reconstruct sensor-specific pixel detail, align each image only with its co-registered twin, or rely on large transformers with 118-173M parameters (and up to 398M). We introduce RS-JEPA, a compact joint-embedding predictive framework built on a Vision Mamba encoder shared by both sensors. Since a state-space encoder reads an image as an ordered sequence of patches, we propose scan-path views, which treat two reading orders of the same image as two views with identical pixels and predict the hidden patches in one order from the visible patches in the other.To keep this prediction challenging, we propose Adversarial View Coupling (AVC), which learns the hardest split of the visible patches, and a neighbourhood consensus loss that aligns the scene similarities of both sensors. Extensive experiments on SAR-optical (BEN-14K, CBRSIR-VS) and PAN-MS (DSRSID) benchmarks demonstrate that RS-JEPA achieves the highest F1@5 among twelve re-implemented methods (72.92, 80.35 and 94.43) with a retrieval network of only 3.88M parameters (14.57M in training, 8-16times fewer than prior JEPA retrievers). Like prior methods, RS-JEPA trains on co-registered pairs. Our results highlight reading order as a source of self-supervised views. code: https://github.com/Tanishq251/RSJEPA.

title: Learning a model of non-stationary nuisances with non-local correlations for object detection
abstract: We tackle the problem of detecting faint objects in multivariate data corrupted by a strong and spatially correlated nuisance component in the low-sample regime. Standard covariance-based models often yield unstable or ill-conditioned estimators of the nuisance statistics, severely degrading detection performance. We propose a data-driven approach based on sparse precision matrix modeling, where the precision matrix is approximated through a pivoted sparse Cholesky factorization whose non-zeros coefficients are learned by maximum likelihood. This yields a low-complexity yet expressive statistical model of the nuisance. Building on this model, we derive a generalized likelihood ratio test for faint source detection enabling direct control of the false alarm rate. The approach is evaluated on an astrophysical application: the detection of exoplanets by high contrast imaging, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: UniFlow-RS: Unified Generative Prediction for Heterogeneous Remote-Sensing Tasks
abstract: Remote-sensing foundation models increasingly unify representations across sensing modalities and downstream tasks, yet their prediction mechanisms remain largely task-specific. Separate decoders, prediction heads, and objectives leave prediction fragmented across tasks. This naturally raises a question: can heterogeneous remote-sensing tasks share the prediction process? UniFlow-RS answers this question with a single latent flow-matching predictor shared across tasks. This requires addressing two key challenges: unifying heterogeneous prediction spaces and harmonizing joint optimization across tasks. First, we cast heterogeneous task outputs into structured visual targets in a common latent space, allowing them to be modeled by the same pretrained flow predictor. Task-dependent conditioning further accommodates differences in input configurations. Second, we optimize all tasks with a common Flow Matching objective, eliminating task-specific prediction losses. To mitigate optimization mismatch across tasks and modalities, we introduce Task-Modality Adaptive Timestep Sampling (TMAS), which dynamically allocates training timesteps according to the online learning state of each task-modality group. Using a single shared model, UniFlow-RS handles six tasks and thirteen datasets, surpassing recent task-specific state-of-the-art methods on several benchmarks while remaining competitive on the others. Beyond these benchmarks, the same checkpoint demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer across unseen datasets, task settings, occlusion conditions, and near-infrared false-color imagery, without target-specific adaptation. Codes are available at https://github.com/MindVision-AI/UniFlow-RS.

title: Joint Quantization and Dynamic Partitioning for Context-Aware Edge Vision Transformers
abstract: Deploying vision transformer models across connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) requires joint management of computation and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. Static split-inference methods use fixed partition points and cannot adapt to time-varying link bandwidth, processing load, and concurrent multi-stream traffic. This paper proposes an edge orchestration framework that jointly selects model partition points, per-layer quantization bitwidths, and execution placement across heterogeneous vehicular compute nodes. The joint partitioning and mixed-precision allocation problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) that minimizes compute and communication energy subject to end-to-end latency and task-quality constraints. The framework is evaluated on Jetson Orin Nano (8~GB), Jetson Orin NX (16~GB), and Jetson AGX Orin (32~GB) nodes using OPV2V-driven multi-stream workloads with $K \in \{2,4,6,8\}$. Across the evaluated configurations, the proposed formulation reduces V2V communication energy by $33.3$--$36.0\%$ relative to a Uniform INT8 split. At $K=8$, end-to-end task completion latency is reduced by $34.0\%$ on the Orin Nano and $33.1\%$ on the Orin NX relative to the same baseline, while limiting the reduction in 3D detection accuracy to $3.1$--$4.1$ percentage points in $\mathrm{mAP}_{50}$ relative to FP16 execution.

title: CroCoMAE: Cross-modal self-supervised collaborative representation learning for SAR-optical remote sensing data
abstract: Remote sensing increasingly captures the Earth's surface through complementary sensors such as SAR and optical, yet ground-truth annotations remain scarce, limiting supervised approaches. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses the label scarcity, and cross-modal SSL further exploits the complementarity between co-located sensors, but existing cross-modal frameworks align modalities mostly through global image-level representations or treat them as largely redundant, leaving their fine-grained complementary structure underexploited. We propose CroCoMAE, a cross-modal SSL framework for SAR-optical remote sensing that unifies contrastive learning and masked image modeling within a ViT-based architecture, operating at two complementary levels. At the image level, an intra-modality contrastive loss on the class token yields globally discriminative, augmentation-invariant representations. At the patch level, masked image modeling drives fine-grained per-modality representations, while a cross-modal contrastive objective aligns a shared subspace across SAR and optical patch tokens, leaving the complementary subspace unconstrained to retain modality-specific information. On two SAR-optical benchmarks covering scene classification and semantic segmentation, CroCoMAE improves over uni-modal SSL baselines and outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal frameworks in most configurations, with gains in both single-modality and multi-modal evaluation across varying label regimes and the largest improvements on semantic segmentation.

title: Obscured Wildfire Flame Detection by Spatio-temporal Analysis of Smoke Patterns Using Frame-wise Transformers
abstract: In this paper, we propose a new paradigm in wildfire management for detecting both visible and obscured fire using Deep Learning (DL). The essence of our method is the joint spatial and temporal analysis of RGB videos, embracing the fact that temporal patterns of smoke motions in consecutive video frames can indicate obscured fire flames. This perspective contrasts the traditional approach of independently analyzing images and individual video frames. To this end, we propose a frame-wise transformer architecture that applies an attention mechanism between the consecutive frames while preserving spatial information within frames as opposed to regular attention mechanisms like the non-local block, which combines spatial and temporal information into a single vector. We also optimize the temporal pattern lengths under different spatial resolutions to achieve the highest performance while reducing the computational cost. To investigate the applicability of our method in aerial image processing, we applied it to a curated version of the FLAME2 dataset that includes dual-mode RGB/IR videos. The IR video feed is used to extract ground truth, while the model is trained only on RGB videos to maintain applicability to lowcost commercial drones (which are equipped only with regular cameras) and facilitate processing existing RGB-only datasets. Our proposed method achieves a Segmentation Foreground Dice score of 92.61%, an Object Detection Precision and Recall rate of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%, respectively. We also investigated the efficacy and generalizability of our method through ablation study

title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.

title: HiPFuse: Real-Time LiDAR Semantic Segmentation for Robotic Perception on Edge Devices
abstract: Real-time robotic perception requires accurate LiDAR semantics under limited resources. Bird's-eye-view (BEV) aggregation is efficient but can mix differently labeled surfaces in columns. We present HiPFuse, a point-BEV fusion framework that exchanges point and height-partitioned BEV features across horizontal scales, combining point-wise detail with 2D spatial context from one LiDAR scan. Fixed height assignments preserve separate vertical aggregation groups, with auxiliary supervision of initial BEV features using targets from the same 3D cells. A dual-scale BEV context module adds broader context from a coarser grid. On SemanticKITTI and MCD, HiPFuse achieves 63.7% and 62.5% mIoU at 14.2 and 22.4 FPS on Jetson AGX Orin, respectively, exceeding the 10 Hz scan rate. Separate training and evaluation show indoor applicability. Replacing only the baseline semantic front end with HiPFuse in fixed robotic systems reduces odometry absolute trajectory error RMSE by 10.6% on average across two outdoor sequences and increases accepted-loop recall by 8.7 percentage points on SemanticKITTI. Qualitative semantic maps show more continuous road labeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/haiyang2022/HiPFuse.

title: Towards Text-Only Remote Sensing Scene Classification via Semantic Proxy
abstract: Remote sensing scene classification (RSSC) is traditionally formulated as a vision-centric problem, where inference relies on rich visual representations extracted from images. In this work, we revisit this assumption by introducing text-only RSSC, a new problem setting that investigates whether remote sensing scenes can be recognized using only textual semantic representations. To enable this study, we propose SeProRS, which reformulates RSSC as a text-only classification task through semantic proxy generation. Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) is first employed to convert remote sensing images into textual descriptions, termed semantic proxies, which are then encoded by a text embedding model for scene classification. This decoupled pipeline provides a unified and reproducible benchmark for evaluating text-only scene understanding. Furthermore, we investigate representative prompting strategies and proxy generators, and analyze their impact on classification performance, text embedding behavior, cross-generator transferability, and efficiency. Extensive experiments on three well-known RSSC datasets show that semantic proxies can preserve substantial discriminative information, while also revealing inherent limitations of purely text-based scene understanding. This paper does not aim to replace image-based RSSC, but instead establishes a new research direction by quantifying the feasibility and boundaries of semantic proxy-based scene recognition. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a foundation for future research on efficient and modality-reduced remote sensing scene understanding. The source code and datasets will be accessible at https://github.com/sstary/SSRS.

title: Relaxing Cross-Modal Correspondence for Multimodal Remote Sensing Pretraining
abstract: Multimodal remote sensing pretraining commonly relies on exact instance-level correspondence across modalities, implicitly treating strictly paired observations as a prerequisite for learning transferable representations. In this work, we revisit this assumption by relaxing cross-modal correspondence from the instance level to the semantic level. We introduce Semantic Pairing (SemPair), a pairing-relaxed pretraining strategy that replaces exact instance pairs with class-consistent cross-instance pairs. To characterize the effect of correspondence relaxation, we formulate a latent-factor model that separates cross-modal dependence into shared semantic structure and instance-specific correlation, showing that SemPair preserves the former while marginalizing instance-specific cross-modal correlations in expectation. We further introduce Mixed Pairing (MixPair) as a controlled interpolation between semantic and exact pairing to study correspondence granularity along a continuous spectrum. Extensive experiments consistently show that SemPair achieves transfer performance comparable to exact pairing (ExaPair), while MixPair reveals a non-monotonic relationship between downstream transfer and the instance-pairing ratio. These results demonstrate that exact instance correspondence is not a prerequisite for effective multimodal remote sensing pretraining and establish cross-modal correspondence granularity as an important design dimension for transferable multimodal representation learning. More broadly, this finding suggests a practical route toward scaling multimodal pretraining with reduced dependence on costly instance-aligned data.

title: DisasterAgent: An Evidence-Driven Agent for Verifiable Disaster Report Generation From Remote Sensing Imagery
abstract: Remote sensing disaster assessment is moving from simple damage classification toward comprehensive report-level analysis. In this setting, responders need not only damage descriptions but also verifiable evidence to guide response and recovery. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) and tool-augmented agents offer strong multimodal reasoning and perception, but they struggle to provide the evidence required for high-stakes verification. To address these limitations, we propose DisasterAgent, an evidence-driven agent that uses a Perception-Augmentation-Generation workflow to generate verifiable disaster reports from bitemporal optical imagery. DisasterAgent first invokes a specialized vision expert toolkit in the perception phase to build a Spatiotemporal Perception Graph (STPG), serving as a structured memory to store and organize disaster-induced changes across space and time. Evidence-based Augmentation (EA) then extracts evidence from the STPG, attaching inline citations that form a closed evidence loop from each statement to the supporting visual evidence. Extensive experiments on the DisasterM3 and RSCC benchmarks demonstrate that DisasterAgent consistently outperforms general-domain VLMs, remote sensing-specialized models, and existing remote sensing agents. Notably, compared with the original model, it improves the average score for disaster report generation on DisasterM3 by 13.5\% and ST5-SCS on RSCC by 15.34\%, providing a more accurate and verifiable solution for disaster emergency response. The code will be available at https://github.com/ZhijianLi2003/DisasterAgent.

title: Overcoming Dynamic Range Limitations in Computational Hyperspectral Imaging
abstract: Computational hyperspectral imaging offers compact spectral sensing, yet imaging high-dynamic-range (HDR) scenes remains challenging. Accurate spectral reconstruction requires encoded measurements to remain within the calibrated linear-response range and above the noise floor. Due to unequal spectral responsivities across the encoding mask, individual channels reach their reliability limits at vastly different incident signal levels. Measurement reliability therefore depends on both exposure time and encoding channel, making it challenging for a single exposure to preserve spectral information in highlights and shadows simultaneously. Here, we demonstrate a physics-guided multi-exposure fusion framework that operates directly in the encoded measurement domain. An analytical reliability prior and learned spatially varying, channel-specific adjustments jointly determine adaptive fusion weights. Measurement-domain spectral-angle supervision further constrains relative channel responses for downstream spectral inversion. The set-wise formulation accommodates varying numbers and configurations of input exposures. We further implement the framework on a 9-channel broadband-encoded stochastic hyperspectral camera, incorporating full-field sensor-response characterization and channel-aware reliability gating. Simulated HDR benchmarks show lower reconstruction errors than representative fusion methods, while controlled spectral measurements and practical HDR scenes confirm improved spectral fidelity and extended usable dynamic range. Measurements using an optical-density target further establish a 16.0-dB increase in spectral reconstruction dynamic range relative to the best fixed single exposure.

title: Earth Embeddings in Environmental Remote Sensing
abstract: Earth observations from satellite platforms have profoundly transformed research and applications across numerous domains. However, uneven observation coverage and frequent data gaps continue to limit their ability to capture Earth's surface dynamics. Moreover, processing multi-modal Earth observations requires substantial computational resources and sophisticated data harmonization frameworks, which may not be readily accessible to many remote sensing practitioners. Earth embeddings have emerged as promising solutions to these challenges. As general-purpose representations converted from multi-source Earth observations, Earth embeddings can support a wide range of downstream tasks with no requirement of task-specific feature design and preprocessing. In this study, we first introduce the theoretical foundations of Earth embeddings. Then, we review several representative Earth embedding products. We next examine the applications of Earth embeddings across six major domains of environmental remote sensing. Finally, we systematically assess the performance of Earth embeddings in four downstream tasks, including hyperspectral image classification, individual tree crown segmentation, crop yield prediction, and aboveground biomass mapping. Our review and case studies suggest that, despite several advantages over conventional Earth observation data, current Earth embeddings do not always outperform remote sensing imagery or hand-crafted features. Earth embeddings should not be viewed as a direct replacement for conventional EO data, but rather as representations that provide stable information across space and time. Remote sensing practitioners may consider evaluating Earth embeddings' suitability for specific tasks and using them strategically, rather than assuming superior performance by default.

title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

title: AdaFCP: Local Neural Functional Representations for Industrial Change Detection
abstract: Industrial sensor measurements often form ordered functional profiles in which persistent operating-regime changes may be confined to short within-cycle regions. Fixed projections can dilute such changes, whereas data-adaptive representation learning complicates reliable statistical testing. This paper proposes adaptive functional change-point detection (AdaFCP) for retrospective detection of a single functional mean change. A compact window and neural basis learn a change-sensitive functional projection by matching the CUSUM path of projected scores to single-change templates. Standardized peak-CUSUM scanning then provides the detection statistic and transition estimate, while the fitted weights identify the contributing within-cycle region. Theoretical analysis characterizes the population path-matching signal and derives an optimal-direction signal-to-noise benchmark. Full-pipeline permutation calibration accounts for adaptive representation learning and restart selection, providing finite-sample false-positive control under exchangeability. A decision-preserving early-stopping variant, AdaFCP-ES, further reduces calibration effort without altering the fixed-budget test decision. Simulations demonstrate advantages over several fixed representations for localized oscillatory changes, while strong analytic and multiscale controls remain competitive. Applications to injection-molding pressure profiles and a nuisance-matched hydraulic benchmark illustrate transition localization and interpretable within-cycle diagnostics, while highlighting the need for dependence-aware calibration in naturally ordered industrial data.

title: CoatFusion: Controllable Material Coating in Images
abstract: Material Coating is a novel image editing task that simulates applying a thin material layer to a target surface (substrate) while preserving the substrate's geometry and shading. Material coating is fundamentally different from material transfer, which typically reinterprets an object as being made of a new material and can modify its shape or overwrite fine details. We introduce CoatFusion , a diffusion-based framework for controllable material coating in images. Since real paired before/after coating data is difficult to acquire, we construct DataCoat110K , a synthetic paired dataset of approximately 110K examples rendered with physically motivated coating layers, including opaque, metallic, and transmissive appearances. CoatFusion formulates coating as visual in-context learning over a triptych containing the substrate image, a canonical 2D albedo texture, and the coated result, and uses cycle-consistent compose/decompose supervision to encourage substrate preservation and geometry-aware texture wrapping. Learned material tokens provide continuous control over roughness and thickness, and discrete on/off control over metalness and transmission. Across held-out synthetic evaluations, real-image examples, ablations, and a human study, CoatFusion produces more realistic and controllable coatings than material transfer/editing baselines and classical blending operations. Code and data for this paper are available at https://github.com/sagielevy/coatFusion.

title: Anisotropic Green Coordinates
abstract: We live in a world filled with anisotropy, a ubiquitous characteristic of both natural and engineered systems. In this study, we concentrate on space deformation and introduce Anisotropic Green Coordinates (AGC), which provide versatile effects for cage-based and variational deformations in both two and three dimensions. The AGC are derived from the anisotropic Laplace equation ∇ • (A∇ u ) = 0, where A is a symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrix. This equation belongs to the class of constant-coefficient second-order elliptic equations, exhibiting properties analogous to the Laplace equation but incorporating the matrix A to characterize anisotropic behavior. Based on this equation, we establish the boundary integral formulation, which is subsequently discretized to derive the deformation coordinates defined on the vertices and normals of oriented simplicial cages. Our method satisfies basic properties such as linear reproduction and translation invariance, and possesses closed-form expressions for both 2D and 3D scenarios. We also give an intuitive geometric interpretation of the approach, demonstrating that our method can generate a quasi-conformal mapping. We demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that the deformation effect is more pronounced when the normal of the cage face aligns with the eigenvector corresponding to the larger eigenvalue of A. This indicates that anisotropy amplifies the deformation sensitivity along this direction, enabling more targeted cage design and matrix selection. Furthermore, we derive the gradients and Hessians of the deformation coordinates and employ the local-global optimization framework to facilitate variational shape deformation, enabling flexible shape manipulation while achieving as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) shape deformation. Experimental results demonstrate that AGC offer versatile and diverse deformation options, providing artists with enhanced flexibility and introducing a novel perspective on spatial deformation. The source code is available at https://github.com/Submanifold/AGC.

title: ProAct: Harnessing Streaming Motion Generation and Agentic Reasoning for Realtime Embodied Social Interaction
abstract: Real-time embodied social interaction places two equally demanding requirements on an agent: continuously generating fluent multimodal interaction behavior, and proactively reasoning over accumulated dialogue and visual context to decide when to take initiative. These requirements must both be satisfied under a strict latency budget, making them difficult to meet simultaneously. We present ProAct , a dual-system framework that manages these time-critical requirements by integrating a low-latency Behavioral System for streaming multimodal interaction with a slower Cognitive System that performs long-horizon social reasoning and produces high-level proactive intentions. The Cognitive System incorporates an efficient memory mechanism and a user-motivation prediction module to reason over accumulated dialogue and visual context and determine when proactive intervention is appropriate. The Behavioral System further includes an intention-conditioned streaming flow-matching motion generator with a disentangled Control-Net branch, which translates deliberative intentions into continuous nonverbal behavior without disrupting interaction fluency.
